pharm: Blood schizonticidal cinchona alkaloid active against erythrocytic forms of Plasmodium falciparum
quick: 648 mg (two capsules) every 8 hours for 7 days
Take with food to minimise gastric upset
Use only if benefit justifies risk; untreated malaria is dangerous
Small amounts in milk; generally compatible, avoid in G6PD-deficient infant
Severe impairment: loading 648 mg then 324 mg every 12 h
No change in mild-moderate; contraindicated in severe (Child-Pugh C)
ECG (QT), CBC/platelets, glucose, signs of cinchonism
summary: Quinine sulfate is a cinchona alkaloid indicated only for treatment of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, including chloroquine-resistant regions. It carries a boxed warning for serious, sometimes fatal haematologic reactions (thrombocytopenia, HUS/TTP) and must not be used for nocturnal leg cramps. Characteristic toxicities include cinchonism and QT prolongation.
indications: Treatment of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, including chloroquine-resistant strains

dosage.d: Loading 648 mg, then 324 mg every 12 hours
dosage.n: First maintenance dose 12 h after load

admin: Take with food to minimise gastric upset
Swallow capsules whole; do not crush (very bitter, irritant)
Not approved for severe/complicated malaria, malaria prophylaxis, or leg cramps
moa: Quinine is a blood schizonticide. It concentrates in the parasite's acidic food vacuole and is thought to interfere with haem detoxification (inhibiting haem polymerisation to haemozoin), causing accumulation of toxic free haem that kills the intra-erythrocytic plasmodium.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to quinine, quinidine or mefloquine; prior quinine-induced thrombocytopenia/TTP/HUS

preg: Malaria in pregnancy carries serious maternal and fetal risk, so treatment should not be withheld. Quinine has been used in pregnancy; use only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk, and monitor for hypoglycaemia.
lact: Quinine is excreted in human milk in small amounts and is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; avoid in infants with known G6PD deficiency.
renal: In severe chronic renal impairment, use a loading dose of 648 mg then 324 mg every 12 hours for 7 days. Effects of mild-moderate impairment are not well characterised; monitor closely.
hepatic: No dose adjustment in mild (Child-Pugh A) or moderate (Child-Pugh B) impairment, but monitor closely for adverse effects. Contraindicated in severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment.

major: QT-prolonging drugs (antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics) - additive QT prolongation
Mefloquine - increased risk of ECG abnormalities and seizures
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ritonavir, ketoconazole) - increased quinine levels/toxicity
moderate: Antacids containing aluminium - reduced quinine absorption
minor: May raise plasma levels of some CYP2D6 substrates
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI upset; avoid grapefruit juice (CYP3A4)
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - may worsen CNS adverse effects
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor ECG (QT), platelets/CBC and blood glucose during therapy

common: Cinchonism: tinnitus, headache, nausea, dizziness, blurred vision
serious: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome / thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

monitoring: Platelet count and complete blood count
Visual and auditory function with prolonged/high exposure
counsel: Take with food and complete the full 7-day course
Report ringing in the ears, deafness, visual changes or unusual bruising/bleeding
This medicine is not for leg cramps or malaria prevention
Seek urgent care for palpitations, fainting, or signs of low blood sugar
pk: Antimalarial effect within hours of dosing
Plasma Tmax approximately 1-3 hours after oral dose
Approximately 11-18 hours in healthy adults (prolonged in malaria)
Store at 20-25 C; protect from light and moisture
pearls: Boxed warning: serious/fatal haematologic reactions (thrombocytopenia, HUS/TTP)
Do NOT use for nocturnal leg cramps - risk outweighs benefit
Hallmark toxicities: cinchonism (tinnitus, headache, visual disturbance) and QT prolongation
Avoid in G6PD deficiency, long QT, myasthenia gravis and optic neuritis
Can cause hypoglycaemia (stimulates insulin release) - monitor glucose
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose; do not double up. Complete the full course.
overdose: Quinine overdose is potentially fatal. Features include cinchonism, cardiotoxicity (QRS/QT widening, arrhythmias, hypotension), CNS depression, seizures and irreversible visual loss (blindness). Management is supportive with cardiac monitoring; multiple-dose activated charcoal may help; treat arrhythmias and seizures. Forced diuresis is not beneficial.
